newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-LORD GYLLENE CONTINUES BROOKSHAW FAMILY SAGA.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-LORD GYLLENE CONTINUES BROOKSHAW FAMILY SAGA.

text.p: Lord Gyllene's 25-length Grand National victory on Monday wrote another chapter in the Brookshaw family saga.
Winning trainer Steve Brookshaw, a former amateur jockey, was enjoying the biggest victory by far of his short training career.
His father, Peter, won a race at Aintree in 1950 and his brother trained a big winner at the Cheltenham Festival in 1984.
But most famous of all, his late uncle Tim, a champion jump jockey in the 1950s, finished a gallant second here on Wyndburgh, riding the last third of the course without a saddle.
But in 1963 he was paralysed in a fall at Aintree.
Brookshaw said on Monday: "This is my second season as a trainer and I couldn't ask for anything better.
"Uncle Tim just missed the ride on a winner. His leather broke and he rode bareback from Becher's Brook to the finish, so he was unlucky."
Brookshaw, delighted with Lord Gyllene, said: "I always thought he would run very well because we know he stays the trip and he was carrying a lot less weight than in the Midlands National."
He added: "He's run his race. He's always had them just behind them and he's murdered them really."
Winning owner Stan Clarke, 63, bought Lord Gyllene after seeing a videotape of him race when the New Zealand-bred horse was still in his home country.
"That's the way I do things," said Clarke, a self-made man who is chairman of Newcastle and Uttoxeter racecourses.
"I also breed horses and have bred two or three winners but I buy most in New Zealand."
Clarke, who started work when he was nine, had two jobs when he was 11, working for a butcher and a chemist.
He told reporters: "Now I own a company worth 51 million pounds ($81 million) and another worth 100 million ($162 million) plus a Grand National winner who is the joy of my life."

Victory was also sweet for 24-year-old Tony Dobbin, who landed the top job as stable jockey to Gordon Richards three years ago only to find himself replaced on the stable star One Man by champion Richard Dunwoody.
Dobbin, thrilled with Lord Gyllene, said: "I fell in my first National and have missed the last three through injury. I've had a few winners over the Aintree fences, but I just can't believe this."
